title: Interpreting Language Reward Models via Contrastive Explanations

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to make black-box language reward models (RMs) more transparent and trustworthy by explaining binary response comparisons, addressing the lack of direct meaning in scalar outputs and the absence of prior XAI techniques applied to RMs. No prior paper explicitly addresses this specific objective. Papers like [1], [3], [4], [5], [6], [12], and [18] discuss explainability and counterfactuals for general machine learning models but do not target reward models or their binary comparisons. Papers [21], [22], and [28] focus on reward models but do not address their interpretability or transparency. Thus, the purpose is **uncovered**.

### Mechanism
The contribution adapts the contrastive-explanation paradigm (counterfactuals and semifactuals) to RM binary comparisons using a two-step attribute-conditioned LLM prompting strategy. Papers [1], [3], [4], [5], [10], [11], [12], [16], [17], [18], and [24] all discuss counterfactual generation methods, including LLM-based approaches ([1], [16]) and attribute-conditioned perturbations ([10], [24]). While the specific implementation (15 attributes, binary RM comparisons) is new, the underlying primitive of generating counterfactuals and semifactuals via perturbations is **covered**.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its method quantitatively on three open-source human-preference datasets, three OpenAssistant RMs, and 150 test comparisons, using syntactic/semantic distances and comparison baselines (Polyjuice, random GPT-4o perturbation). Papers [1], [7], [8], [9], [12], [16], [19], [23], and [27] discuss evaluation methods for XAI systems, including metrics like semantic similarity, syntactic distance, and comparison against baselines. The evaluation design (benchmarking perturbation-based explanations with metrics and baselines) is **covered**.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM alignment and reward-model interpretability. Papers [21], [22], and [28] address reward models and their alignment with human preferences, while papers [1], [3], [4], [5], [6], [12], [18], and [24] address interpretability and explainability in machine learning models. Although no prior paper combines these two areas, both domains are individually **covered**.

## Purpose

The purpose is to turn local explanations into generalized, actionable insight about RM (reward model) behaviour and enable comparison across RMs.

Papers [2] (GALE: Globally Assessing Local Explanations), [4] (Global Explanations with Local Scoring), [13] (GLEAMS: Bridging the Gap Between Local and Global Explanations), [17] (Learning Global Transparent Models from Local Contrastive Explanations), and [22] (From local counterfactuals to global feature importance) all share the objective of aggregating local explanations into global insights. Paper [2] explicitly aims to "globally assess local explanations." Paper [22] explicitly frames the purpose as "From local counterfactuals to global feature importance." The objective of turning local explanations into global/generalized insight is well-covered. The "comparison across RMs" sub-purpose is more specific, but the primary objective (local→global) is clearly covered.

## Mechanism

The mechanism involves: (1) aggregating CFs/SFs over many comparisons to compute Preference Flip Rate (PFR) as a global sensitivity measure; (2) ranking attributes per RM and comparing RMs via Kendall's tau over ranking vectors; (3) a workflow extracting representative examples.

Paper [22] explicitly uses "local counterfactuals to global feature importance" by aggregating counterfactuals — the same primitive of aggregating local CFs to get global sensitivity. Paper [2] (GALE) aggregates local explanations globally. Paper [4] uses local scoring to derive global explanations. For the Kendall's tau comparison of ranking vectors, papers [3], [9], [10], [25] all use Kendall's tau for comparing feature importance rankings. Paper [5] (Confident Feature Ranking) and [25] (Statistical Significance of Feature Importance Rankings) both rank features and compare rankings. The combination is partially covered: aggregating CFs for global sensitivity is in [22], and Kendall's tau for ranking comparison is in [3]/[9]/[10]. The specific PFR metric (flip rate as sensitivity) is somewhat novel, but the underlying primitive of "count how often flipping an attribute changes the output" is a standard sensitivity/flip-rate measure seen in counterfactual literature broadly.

## Evaluation

The evaluation design involves computing PFR profiles across 500 comparisons per dataset, filtered to agreement cases, and comparing profiles across models (Figure 3 style). This is essentially a sensitivity analysis / feature importance profile comparison across models — a standard evaluation design seen in papers [20] (Comparison of feature importance measures), [2] (GALE), and [22]. The design of comparing feature importance rankings across models using standard metrics is covered by [20] and [2].

## Domain

The domain is reward-model interpretability. Prior papers focus on general ML model interpretability, NLP models ([6]: Local vs. Global interpretations for NLP), and neural networks. None of the prior papers specifically address reward models used in RLHF/preference learning. However, under the special rule, reward models are a specific instance within the broader ML model interpretability area, which is extensively covered. The domain facet should be COVERED.
